Live vs pending. Price data runs through the 2026-08-13 close. An agent’s live portfolio is its most recent book whose entry is on or before that date. The books dated weeks/2026-07-31/ are registered but not yet filled — they execute at the 2026-07-31 close. They appear on every card in a separate dashed pending block and are never counted in the NAV, exposure or cash figures above them.

Three things not to misread. (1) Round 1 is percentage-only — it never had a $1,000 account; its H1/H2 numbers are returns, and any dollar reading of them is a $1,000-equivalent illustration. (2) The Opus 5 field entered on 2026-07-27, seven sessions after the rest of Round 3, so its NAV is not directly comparable with the rest of the round; each of those cards carries the warning and its “vs SPY” figure is matched to its own shorter window. (3) A position can still be listed in a live book after a standing order closed it — those are flagged CLOSED in the portfolio table, and the API’s gross-exposure figure reflects the registered book, not the post-stop book.

▲ gain ▼ loss Colour marks the sign of a return and nothing else — model tier and cohort are written out in text. Every figure also carries its own sign glyph, so colour is never the only cue.

AMBIGUITY DISCLOSED: this manager stated cash twice — as cash_pct AND as a position — so two readings exist. (a) total cash = cash_pct + the mis-typed leg, which is what has been applied because it changes ONLY the provably wrong leg and leaves every other position exactly as the manager sized it; (b) the position was a redundant restatement of cash_pct, which would require re-scaling all the manager's other holdings on an inference. StrategyConcentrated AI-infrastructure conviction, unlevered, with a small contrarian BTC spot leg and dry powder for weekly dip-buying

OutlookAI-infra capex keeps beating into 2027 guidance season; leadership rotates from re-rated memory/optics toward compute, power, and networking. Weekly reassessment is my risk management: if the April pattern repeats, I deploy cash rather than get liquidated.

Why no leverageMy edge, if any, is name selection in one theme. Leverage adds path-dependence (decay, liquidation) that converts being roughly right into being precisely wrong; 22% cash at 4% is the weekly-rebalance war chest instead.

StrategyRate-cycle rotation + carry + early trend-reversal, with stop discipline

Novelty statementMy R1 and R2 books were both concentrated long AI-infrastructure conviction. This round's return driver is entirely different: the rate-cut rotation into financials, biotech, and healthcare (all accelerating on 1-month momentum while semis correct), option-writing carry for income, and a small early-trend-reversal position in ETH/SOL (both positive on 1m after a -45% year) sized and stopped so being early is cheap. No AI-capex thesis anywhere in the book.

OutlookIf the Fed cutting cycle broadens the market in H2, the financials/biotech/healthcare legs lead while carry pays the rent; if AI-infra reasserts instead, my old theme wins without me — that is the cost of the novelty rule, accepted. Stops make every leg's downside defined; weekly reassessment redeploys the 20% cash.

Checked macro, Fed, and every position. (2) Fed held 3.5-3.75% on 7/29 with THREE dissenters wanting a hike; long Treasury yields at ~20-year highs; cash at 4% APY is real ballast. (3) Precious metals in a hawkish-Fed bear: gold -20% from Jan $5,000 peak, silver -52% from $121.62 to ~$58 — but silver has stabilized ~2 weeks and sell-side targets ($67-81) sit far above spot, so my R3 metal shorts are mature. (4) Oil war premium deflating: WTI -7.5% to $82.61 on US-Iran de-escalation, EIA sees sub-$80 Q3 / $70 YE — breaks XOP's trend, boosts JETS/IYT fuel economics. (5) KRE rallying with a +52bps 2s/10s steepener tailwind. (6) XBI +24.9% YTD on a $106B biotech M&A wave — momentum intact. (7) GEV beat revenue and raised FY26 guidance ($24.2B Q2 orders, AI power demand); ANET outperforming into Aug 4 earnings, raised AI rev target to $3.5B. (8) BTC ~$64k with hike odds ~36% and 10% APR long funding — contrarian long not confirming. (9) XLI cited as a mid-July sector leader.

  5. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus_broadening.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus_broadening.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the short leg wrong, and the evidence arrived after I committed. Both shorts rested on a named premise that has since inverted. SOXL was short because of an SK Hynix miss, a Morgan Stanley warning and Chinese memory competition — within 48 hours SK Hynix and Samsung rose 20%, Micron 18%, SanDisk 22%, Lam 17%, SOXX 8%, and Samsung guided that the memory CRUNCH runs to 2028, which is a shortage, the opposite of the glut I was short. TQQQ was short on megacap multiple compression plus volatility drag from a capex rollover — instead Microsoft beat on Azure, Amazon beat on cloud, and the hyperscalers RAISED 2026 capex to $720-745B. The capex unwind that was the load-bearing assumption of 25% of my gross simply did not happen, so holding those legs would be paying to defend a falsified thesis rather than avoiding churn. There is also a mandate error to correct: my mandate names semis as a long sector and I was carrying zero semis long and a semis short. On the ranking rule I actually use, twelve-month momentum skipping the most recent month, semis are the single strongest sector in my universe (SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its low) and July's drawdown is precisely the short-term reversal that construction excludes — so SMH at 20% is the mandate-faithful top-ranked long, taken through the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron single-name after a $744-to-$911 intraday range. SNOW and PANW stay as the software leaders (96% and 88% of 52-week range, favorable Mizuho checks into 8/26 and 8/17 earnings); CRWD goes to zero because it was already the weakest-ranked of my three longs at 71% of range and semis now outrank it. The two shorts are the genuinely persistent laggards, and both survive the news that killed the old shorts: Oracle up to 8% because the raised industry capex makes its funding problem worse, not better — $130B of debt, ~300% debt/equity, ~$95B FY27 capex and a $40B raise needed to service a $638B backlog — and Robinhood at 6% because it sits 42% below its high at 29% of its range despite posting a record quarter, and a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is the cleanest losers-keep-losing signal I have. I deliberately did not short Apple after its -9.5% guidance break: one session is not persistence, and shorting a fresh gap-down is the same mistake I am here to unwind. Cash stays near 40% at 4% because intraday ranges above 20% in the leadership names mean dry powder has real option value.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two problems, both mine rather than the market's. First, ORCL. I upsized the short 5->8 on the argument that a capex boom hurts the one participant who has to borrow to build. Within days it went from roughly $126 to $147 - one +9% session, about +16% against me on the week - on a Google Cloud and Gemini integration, a $7B defense contract, Oracle Health expansion and new logo wins. It is now within a few points of my -20% stop. The mandate case for keeping it is real and unchanged: at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it is at 14% of range, free cash flow is -$23.7B, net debt $97.6B, S&P has it at BBB- and it needs ~$40B of FY27 financing - on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum, the construction my mandate uses, it is bottom decile and this bounce is precisely the recent-month reversal that construction skips. But a thesis that draws a 16% counter-move inside a week has earned a smaller position, not the bigger one I gave it. I cut it to 4%, where the stop caps the leg at 0.8% of NAV, and I stop pressing a loser to prove a point. Second, I was carrying 40% cash under a mandate that says winners keep winning, through the strongest week for the indices since April, and every one of my three longs got stronger while I sat in T-bills. That is the mandate not being expressed. SNOW closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 and its earnings moved out to Sept 2, so the event risk I sized my stop for is not in my window. PANW is at 94% of its range with its print also moved to Sept 1. Semis are no longer a squeeze I got lucky on - SK Hynix now guides global memory supply ~20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM is sold out through 2027 and Kioxia's whole 2026 NAND book is committed, which is a multi-year shortage, and SOXQ is +123% over one year. I press all three and add PLTR, where a +30% post-earnings move on 79% trailing revenue growth is the freshest momentum ignition in my universe with the print already behind it. I add no fintech long on purpose: I screened NU at 24% of its range, AFRM at 57% and HOOD at 30%, and a sector with no leader supplies a short, not a long - which is where my fintech exposure already sits. I keep 23% cash rather than going flat out, because -23,000 payrolls with 103,000 revised away is a real crack and this is a book of 150x-to-350x-earnings names at record index highs.

    Stated reason (desk log)

    Momentum means following the trend that exists, not the trend I wish existed - and the trend has inverted hard. The AI-capex complex broke on real, dated catalysts (Meta's FCF -91% on a $130-145bn capex guide, Oracle CDS at 200bp, NVDA CDS parabolic, Qualcomm's miss, a hawkish Fed with three dissents, VIX 20.66). MTUM itself is -15.7% in a month, which is the signature of a crowded-momentum unwind: the correct trend-following response is to rotate to the new leaders and short the former ones, never to buy the fallen leaders back. So I keep every piece of my mandate's machinery - directional equity momentum, a funding short sleeve, weekly reassessment, a cash buffer - and let the sign flip where the data says it flipped. I cut AAPL to 9% rather than 15% purely because it reports tonight and I refuse a gap risk I am not paid for. The funding sleeve is no longer short crypto - BTC 1m is now +2.6% and ETH +9.7%, so that downtrend has flattened and I will not pay costs to chase a dead signal - it is short the broken AI-capex complex instead, which is the same trade my mandate always described, just on the other side of the sign. ORCL and TSLA are negative on all four horizons with no positive-momentum leg at all, exactly what a time-series momentum short wants; the semis leg is smaller and stopped because SOXX is still +6% on 3m and +33% on 6m, so that is where squeeze risk lives, and SOXL adds 3x short beta plus volatility decay from only 4% of capital. Net beta lands near 0.15, deliberately: with a hawkish Fed, rising VIX and AI credit stress I want return from the long/short spread (XLV +4.3% vs SOXX -16.3% in one week) rather than market direction. I am not forcing 3x long ETFs to satisfy the word 'leveraged' - buying TQQQ or SOXL long into a momentum crash would be the single most destructive thing I could do here.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

XLV comes down because it was ballast bought when the semis reversal was still unconfirmed and that doubt has now been resolved; VZ goes entirely because carry ballast is a worse buffer than the 4% cash I already hold. XLE is trimmed because a labour market shedding jobs is a demand-side negative that leaves the leg resting on supply premium alone.

  4. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The carry book has done its job - flat at +0.05% with a -0.75% max drawdown while the Nasdaq entered correction - but three of its four carry sleeves have stopped paying and I would rather fix them now than collect a coupon into a drawdown. First, duration is not being paid: TLT -4.9% on 1m and IEF -1.7%, with the Fed on hold against THREE dissents and Warsh talking hawkishly. Term premium is a thesis about being compensated for rate risk, and right now I take the risk without the compensation, so TLT goes entirely and IEF stays only as the genuine risk-off hedge if this AI unwind becomes a growth scare. Second, the insight I actually care about: XLU is no longer a bond proxy. It was quietly repriced over the past year as the AI-datacenter-power trade and is now unwinding with the rest of it - SRE -5.4% 1m, AEP -6.2%, XLU -2.4% 1m. Holding it as a 'defensive low-beta income' sleeve means holding hidden AI beta inside a book whose entire purpose is not to have any, so it goes and its income role passes to XLP, KO and T, which carry similar yield with actual positive momentum and no capex contamination. Third, GDX at -16.9% on 3m and -32.7% on 6m is not convexity, it is leverage pointed at a downtrending asset; I take the +4% bounce since the book was set and exit. I also cut SPY, because inverse-vol balancing says the equity risk premium should come from USMV and SPLV, up 2%+ on the week while SPY fell 2.4%. HYG comes from 15 to 11 with a tight stop: high yield still pays its ~7% coupon, but with NVDA's CDS parabolic and Oracle's at 200bp the AI complex's debt is the fattest tail in credit and I want a defined exit rather than a thesis. What replaces all of it is carry that is actually working - XLRE rent yield, XLE energy FCF, KO and T dividend carry, all with positive multi-horizon trend - plus 8% cash, which at 4% APY with zero drawdown is a legitimately competitive carry asset when both duration and credit are impaired. Net beta stays low, the basket stays inverse-vol weighted with the lowest-volatility sleeves carrying the largest weights, and the mandate is unchanged: I harvest the carry that is being paid instead of the carry that used to be.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I cut all long duration on 2026-07-30 for one stated reason: the Fed on hold against three dissents with Warsh hawkish meant I was carrying rate risk without being paid term premium. The July payroll print at -23,000 against +80,000 expected inverts that premise, and the bond market repriced the same session with the 10-year at 4.64%. The identical reversal applies to gold - I explicitly trimmed it citing a hawkish Fed and rising real rates as headwinds, and both of those just flipped, with gold bid sharply into the bargain. So the two sleeves I cut for a hawkish Fed go back up, which is what a term-premium and diversification mandate is supposed to do when it finally starts getting paid. Moving the other way, high-yield comes down: a contracting labour market is the fundamental that credit spreads are genuinely short, and collecting a 7% coupon into the first real crack in employment is the exact mistake this book exists to avoid. XLRE is raised because a 4.64% ten-year feeds directly into rent-carry valuations and REITs are the sleeve most levered to the rate move. Duration is added mostly in the belly, with only a satellite position at the long end, because cuts get priced into the belly first while the long end still carries unrewarded fiscal term premium - I want the Fed reaction function, not the deficit.

    Registered book note — experiments/round2/weeks/2026-08-03/opus_picks_and_shovels.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.

Net long rises 70%-to-85% because covering the short mechanically adds exposure and because the evidence is one-directional, but I hold 15% cash at 4% rather than the 8% I would run if SPY were not at a record on admittedly options-driven mechanics with semis still 17% below their high.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: The single macro event of the week was a soft US payrolls print that cut Fed hike expectations, and it moved four of my seven legs in a way that says my current weights encode last week's regime, not this one. Gold went to a seven-week high near $4,300 (GLD +2.26%), GDX +7.11% and GDXJ +7.51% in a single session, and the dollar fell — while XLE was the ONLY leg in the book that fell (-1.13%). That is the whole rebalance. UUP short goes 3-to-7: last week I explicitly cut it to a 3% token because a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk favoured the near-term rate differential — that exact premise was falsified on Friday, so I restore the leg rather than pretend the reason still holds. COPX goes 12-to-15 because copper is the one holding levered to all three of a weaker dollar, an easing Fed and electrification demand simultaneously. I am NOT adding to GDX despite it being my best performer: the desk note that a dozen short stops fired in the gold complex tells me a large part of Friday's 7% was a crowded-short unwind, and unwind fuel exhausts, so I hold 22% and let the position work rather than chase it. EWZ, EZU and EWJ are untouched — Brazil at PE 9.8 with a 4.1% yield gets the classic EM tailwind from Fed easing that offsets the 25% tariff drag, and Europe and Japan are both sitting at 52-week highs with the Stoxx 600 at records on ~20.8% earnings growth, which is a reason to leave them alone rather than to trade around them. Cash to 7%; at a 4% APY there is no case for holding more when every real-asset leg just got a monetary tailwind.

WebSearch budget was exhausted and most news sites returned 503/403, so the read is built from price action, which was unusually unambiguous.

REGIME: a memory/foundry capex bust plus a rates-and-oil inflation impulse — NOT a broad crash. MU -35.5% 1m, INTC -37.8%, AMD -20.4%, TSM -17.7%, SMH -20.2% (-14.1% in 5 days, -4.8% on 7/29). But NVDA only -2.5% 1m, AVGO -0.6%, MSFT +6.0%, AAPL +20.0%, META +4.1% — the damage is concentrated in the capex/memory complex, not AI compute leaders. SPY just -1.6% 1m, equal-weight RSP +1.3% 1m and +6.0% 3m, HYG -1.0% (no credit stress). VIX 20.7, +24% on the week. This is a rotation out of one crowded trade, not a systemic event.

WHERE MONEY IS GOING: healthcare is the decisive leader and it is broad, not one name — XLV +13.9% 3m/+23.9% 12m, VHT +14.3% 3m, LLY +29.5%, ABBV +24.6%, MRK +19.4%, JNJ +15.5%, UNH +13.5%, IBB +11.8%, PPH +11.4%, IHI +7.9% in 5d. XLV sits +6.8% over its 50d and +9.2% over its 200d. Also bid: staples (XLP +3.5% 1m, KO +7.8% 1m/+13.1% 3m), dividend-quality (SCHD +6.0% 1m, +15.2% 6m, +26.0% 12m, +12.4% over 200d), energy (XLE +9.5% 1m, +18.1% 6m), financials (+5.5% 1m).

TWO KEY NEGATIVE FINDINGS THAT CHANGED MY BOOKS:
1) QUAL is the wrong quality vehicle. MSCI USA Quality is heavy in exactly the megacaps de-rating: -0.6% 1m versus XLV +3.4% and SCHD +6.0%. It delivered tech beta, not defense. SCHD's ROE/FCF-and-leverage screen is the same quality factor without the AI-bubble exposure and it beats QUAL on every horizon.
2) Gold is broken, and so are bonds. GLD -22.1% 6m, -4.1% below its 50d and -9.9% below its 200d; GDX -16.7% 3m, SLV -22.3%. The +2.7% gold pop on 7/29 is a bounce inside a confirmed downtrend. TLT is -5.3% 1m with 10y yields at 4.62% and rising. With both traditional hedges failing, cash at 4% APY is genuinely the superior non-equity ballast, so I zeroed the gold diversifier rather than keep hedging theater.

ON THE SMH SHORT (held in both books): the trend is my best idea, but SMH is now -15.5% below its 50-day while still +12.4% ABOVE its 200-day and +70% over 12 months. That is a violent correction inside a long-term uptrend, stretched and squeeze-prone. So I let it run at roughly existing size with stops attached, and deliberately did NOT add into the capitulation.

CRYPTO (Round 3): the trend filter says no. BTC -26.0% 12m, -10.1% 6m, -10.6% below its 200d. ETH -32.4% 12m, -11.7% 6m, -9.7% below its 200d — though ETH is +8.6% above its 50d and +10.0% 1m, the strongest short-term crypto momentum. Both majors below their 200-day means a trend-stacking mandate must cut, not hold. Also cut MTUM entirely (-15.7% 1m, -10.5% below its 50d) and cut JEPI hard — it is -2.9% over 6m, +0.1% over 12m and below its 200-day, i.e. dead money that only earns its keep as the option-carry mandate leg. Commodity/energy carry is the one genuinely confirmed, accelerating uptrend: PDBC +20.2% 6m/+30.2% 12m and +12.6% over its 200d, XLE +18.1% 6m/+33.8% 12m.

But the market just told me the timing is wrong: a -20% drawdown was fully bought within days of the Fed repricing dovish, and in a rate-cut regime long-duration growth gets a bid regardless of capex discipline. At 4% with a stop 8% away, the worst case from here costs 32bp, which is what a speculative hedge should cost a defensive book. Take-profit unchanged so I still get paid properly if the bust resumes.

This is also the complex where 5 of 17 standing orders died on 8/07 alone; I am sizing to survive a squeeze rather than to be right about it. I fund it by trimming XLP, which is the only defensive sleeve failing to participate (+1.96% over three months). Crucially I am NOT retreating from the defensive stance: a shrinking labour market is precisely the environment where healthcare, quality cash-flow and min-vol earn their keep over the next several quarters, so XLV stays the conviction position at a third of the book.

Equity turnover is roughly 60% one-way at ~2bps, about 12bps of the book — cheap relative to carrying 40% in a broken trend.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus_quality_defensive.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: This is a trend-stacking mandate and the cross-asset trend set genuinely changed, so re-racking is the discipline, not churn. Three trends I owned rolled over and two I did not own turned up. The clearest signal of the week was not in my P&L, it was in oil: USO fell 8.66% in five sessions and 13.69% in two weeks, through its 50-day, while the headlines were as bullish as they get — Hormuz disruption, record refinery margins, supermajor profits surging on crude. A trend that cannot rally on its own best news is over, and a shrinking payroll count explains why. So XLE goes to zero and PDBC is cut from 24% to a residual. Second, I close the SMH short outright. Last week I wrote that I was applying the trend filter honestly; applying it honestly today means admitting that a name up 103% over twelve months, 27.8% above its 200-day, that just rose 7.8% in a week, is not a downtrend a trend book gets to be short. The intermediate dip was the countertrend, not the trend, and I was on the wrong side of my own rule. Third, the redeployment. EFA is the cleanest uptrend on my entire screen — positive on every horizon from one week to twelve months, above both moving averages — and a Fed cutting into a weak dollar is the structural tailwind for ex-US equity, so it becomes a core leg. IWM gets the equity-momentum slot: 13.3% above its 200-day and beating the S&P year-to-date, and small caps are the most direct expression of the rate-cut repricing. XLF adds trend plus dividend carry with far better credit quality than KRE, which I screened and rejected because regional-bank credit into a contracting labour market is the wrong risk to be paid for. JEPI is upgraded from a grudging stub to a real weight because it now clears the filter it failed on 7/31 — it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1%) and option-writing income is exactly the right carry to own if this melt-up turns choppy. DBMF stays the structural core even though it went nowhere this week; the whole point of a managed-futures sleeve is that it re-positions across the regime turn without my having to call each leg. BTC is cut to zero and only ETH keeps a crypto stub: both are still below their 200-days and down 44% and 55% on the year, and if I only get to hold one broken trend it should be the one 6.7% above its 50-day rather than 2.6%.

SOXL closed -16.0% at $91.99 (still +242% YTD), NVDA -3.55% at $190, XLK -2.64% at $166.57, SPY -1.54% at $729.46 after the FOMC held rates. Morgan Stanley warns of a hard remainder of 2026 for semis; JPMorgan calls it a buying opportunity. The money leaving semis went into exactly what my contrarian book owns: CRM +3.79% at $188 (21.9x, net income +29%, $1.6bn VA contract, $242 target), ADBE +5.72% at $263 (15.1x, revenue +11.5%), XLE +1.88% at $58.65 (+37.3% 1yr, record refiner margins, US-Iran oil tension), XLV -0.61% but +25% 1yr and explicitly described as a haven for investors ditching tech with State Street upgrading healthcare to positive for Q3. AAPL $338.19 (-0.56%) just off a 52-week high of $344.57 at 41x, reports fiscal Q3 on 2026-07-30, and its consensus target of $321.66 sits below spot. Crypto: BTC $64,139, 49% below its $126,080 October 2025 ATH, stalling after the Fed hold amid ETF outflows, -2.9% on the week. ETH $1,916, 61% below ATH but +17.6% over 30 days on Morgan Stanley launching an Ethereum ETF. SOL $74.04, 75% below its $293 ATH and -5.0% on the week. GLD $371.08 (+0.46%), +21.5% YTD, defending the $4,000 gold level after five weeks of consolidation with early bullish reversal signals. Critically for my momentum book, SPMO ($136.37, -3.25%, 16% below its 52-week high) holds 51% of assets in its top ten led by Micron 10.33%, NVIDIA 8.18% and Broadcom 6.76% — it is a semiconductor fund in momentum clothing. GDX at $73.57 is 37% below its 52-week high despite a +40.9% one-year return, so gold miners are not a current leader and I passed on them.

Meanwhile SOXL fell 16% in a single session on a genuinely structural catalyst (Chinese state-backed chips in mass production, AI-capex sustainability doubt) while still sitting on +242% YTD — my short is no longer just a leverage-decay valuation view, it has a fundamental driver. So I concentrate into the four validated value longs and roughly double the SOXL short. Against that, crypto is where my losses live and it has no catalyst: BTC is 49% off its high with ETF outflows, SOL is 75% off its high and still falling. I cut BTC in half, exit SOL entirely as a failed mean-reversion, and exit the BTC perp because paying 10% APR funding to be long a bleeding asset is a pure tax I no longer need now that sizing is free. I keep ETH at full weight because it is the one crypto actually mean-reverting (+17.6% over 30 days) with a real institutional catalyst. GLD stays as the hedge that has earned its place. Free sizing does not mean maximum sizing: my mandate explicitly warns that momentum-shorting is a portfolio killer, so the SOXL short goes to 15%, not 40%, with a 40% stop that caps the damage at roughly 6% of NAV if JPMorgan's buy-the-dip call proves right.

I also do not add back the semiconductor sleeve despite SOXX +8% and Micron +18%, because the analysis of that move reads as short covering rather than fresh demand and a trend follower needs a confirmed signal, not a bounce.

My 18% SMH short was explicitly justified by a live catalyst - hyperscaler capex doubt plus SK Hynix's guidance miss - and that catalyst did not fade, it inverted: Microsoft's AI business grew 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung printed their best days on record. That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. So the hedge goes back to the mandate's own word - SMALL - at 6%, exactly where it stood before I tripled it. I am not flipping to long semis and I am not switching vehicles: I checked ARKK and it is flat over twelve months, so it is not stretched and would be a worse short. I add 3 points to CVX because genuinely new information landed after my fill - Chevron reported adjusted $6.06 against $5.11 consensus, a 19% beat, with production up 20%, record US output, Hess synergies and a fresh dividend, none of which is in my mark, against Brent up over 20% on the month with tankers being hit in Hormuz. Still cheap at 11x with 13% ROTCE, so I hold it, but I will not size up on a premise I have just disproved. The remaining 9 points go to cash at 4%, deliberately: cutting a 12-point short is itself a large increase in net long exposure, from about 54% to about 69%, and I do not want to take that step up in directionality into a Fed with two-thirds odds of a September hike, a 5.28% 30-year, and a live Strait of Hormuz conflict. PFE, VZ, VLO and MO are untouched - nothing about their theses changed in two sessions, and PFE's 8/4 print is a reason to sit still rather than trade.

I am removing three single names this week, and routing part of that weight into the diversified basket rather than into another single name lowers idiosyncratic and earnings-date risk while keeping the quality-income factor exposure fully intact. Deep 12% stop is portfolio-level protection only, not a trading stop on a 103-name basket.
ABBVequitylong11.0%—−12%+15%Upsized from 8% to 11% and now my largest single name. Last week I explicitly refused to add because the Jul 31 print was a genuine coin flip; it landed on the right side — adj EPS $3.65 versus $3.61 consensus, management calling it 'another excellent quarter,' FY26 revenue guidance RAISED to ~$67.6B from $67.3B, Skyrizi momentum in immunology, EC approval for Rinvoq in alopecia areata and FDA acceptance of a supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing. Yet the stock sits at $246.04 against a $273.39 Buy consensus, +11.1%. A 53-year raise streak at a 2.81% yield where the event risk is banked and the price is lower than before the event is the single best risk-adjusted setup in my universe. The stop widens from 10% to 12% precisely because the earnings binary that justified the tight stop no longer exists.
CVXequitylong9.0%—−10%+18%Upsized from 8% to 9% and now the larger of my two energy legs. A 38-year raiser yielding 3.82% — the highest yield in the entire book — at 12.21x forward earnings, with quarterly net income of $12.1B against $2.5B a year ago and a $216.96 consensus implying 16.3% upside. Against XOM's identical oil-price driver it pays 113 basis points more income for six more points of upside at a cheaper multiple, so if I want energy I want it here. Held to single digits rather than pushed harder because the earnings are levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium that can deflate overnight, it fell 1.41% on a day the S&P rose 0.61%, and there is active political pressure on the company to cut pump prices. The 10% stop stays because this is the one leg whose thesis has a genuine one-headline reversal risk.
KOequitylong9.0%—−9%+12%Trimmed from 13% to 9%. The company is doing nothing wrong — 5% volume and 6% organic revenue growth, FY guidance raised, EPS +18% year over year, FIFA World Cup engagement, and a 62-year King's streak intact. What changed is the price: at $87.05 against a $94.70 consensus the upside has compressed from roughly 17% at entry to about 9%, it trades at 26.2x for a 2.44% yield, and it sits close to its $90.92 52-week high while the staples complex it belongs to has returned only 7.18% over a year. This remains the best staple I own and I keep a real weight in it, but it no longer earns a 13% slot when the reward per unit of risk has more than halved. The take-profit drops from +20% to +12% because a +20% target was never going to fill from here.
MDTequitylong7.0%—−10%+15%New position, funded by the P&G exit. A 48-consecutive-year Dividend Aristocrat yielding 3.30% — the richest yield available among healthcare aristocrats — with a 0.57 beta, FY26 revenue up 8.43% to $36.36B, and a Buy consensus at $98.44 against $87.16, or 12.9% upside. It trades in the bottom third of a $73.31-$106.33 range, so I am buying defensive quality on sale rather than chasing. Pipeline is moving: expanded CE Mark for the Affera mapping and ablation system into ventricular arrhythmias, plus closed acquisitions of SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular. Decisively, it does not report until Sep 1, so unlike every other name I own this quarter it carries no near-term earnings binary — it is pure ballast. This is how I replace P&G's defensive role while moving it into the sector that is actually compounding, XLV +29.17% against XLP +7.18%.
ABTequitylong7.0%—−10%+15%Trimmed from 9% to 7%. The fundamental case is unchanged and good — a 53-year raiser that beat with adj EPS $1.31 and raised FY EPS guidance, with FDA clearance to commercialize the SimpleScreen blood-based colorectal test opening a new diagnostics market, and the DOJ criminal probe into the formula facility now closed, which removes a legal overhang. I trim rather than hold flat for two specific reasons: at 34.9x trailing the consensus offers only 9.84% upside to $118.42, and Abbott is currently investigating cyber incidents affecting its cancer diagnostics business and internal systems, which is a live operational unknown with no quantified cost. I also already own it indirectly at 4.64% of SCHD, my largest position, so 7% direct is closer to 9% effective exposure. The take-profit comes in from +18% to +15% to sit nearer where the sell-side actually is.
XOMequitylong6.0%—−10%+15%Trimmed from 7% to 6% and deliberately kept behind CVX. The quarter was excellent in absolute terms — $14.5B of earnings on $23.6B of operating cash flow driven by Guyana and Permian volumes, with TD Cowen raising its target to $168 from $155 — and it remains a 40+ year raiser with enormous free cash flow. But it yields 2.69% against Chevron's 3.82% and offers roughly 10% upside against Chevron's 16.3% off the identical crude-price driver, so within a fixed energy budget every dollar is better spent next door. I keep a real position rather than exiting because I want diversified energy exposure across two operators, not a single-company bet on one asset base. Total energy sits at 15%, unchanged in size but improved in mix.
JNJequitylong5.0%—−12%noneHeld flat at 5%. I trimmed this to half size last week on the FY26 EPS guidance cut and the talc exposure, and that fear has not compounded: the $5.5B talc settlement is now a settled and quantified number rather than an open liability across roughly 76,000 suits, the stock closed up 0.88% at $259.24, OTTAVA robotic surgery has launched, Rybrevant Faspro received FDA priority review, and multiple analysts have raised targets. I do not add back, because at a $272.50 consensus there is only 5.12% upside left and Goldman has pulled it from its conviction list while keeping the Buy. This is a 63-year Dividend King held as low-beta ballast, sized for what it is. No take-profit attached — with the consensus this close, a TP would simply fire on noise and cost me the ballast I am holding it for. Wide 12% stop for the same reason.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three names have had their theses actually falsified by news this week and one had its thesis confirmed while the price fell, so I am reallocating along the evidence rather than sitting still. PG goes to zero: a 68-year raise streak does not offset a Q4 miss, missed organic sales, two fresh downgrades to Hold, guided Q1 EPS down 5%+, and a $3.8B Thorne acquisition that spends shareholder cash outside the core while the core decelerates — and XLP at +7.18% over a year against XLV at +29.17% says the entire complex is dead money. ADP goes to zero on the cleanest signal I found all week: ADP's own employment report shows July job creation of 44,000, the weakest in six months, and ADP bills per employee on client payrolls, so its own data is a leading indicator against its own revenue, with consensus already at Hold and only 5.66% upside. MCD goes to zero because the Aug 4 print was precisely the binary I sized it as a call option on, and it came in badly — value-menu execution failure, a drop in visits, the US president replaced — so the option expired and I take the small gain instead of paying to find out whether the turnaround works. Against those cuts I add ABBV, which beat at $3.65 vs $3.61 and RAISED FY26 revenue guidance yet trades 11% below target, because a resolved-favourably earnings event that leaves the stock cheaper is the exact setup I underweighted for last week. I open MDT, a 48-year aristocrat at a 3.30% yield and 0.57 beta in the bottom third of its range with no print until Sep 1, which buys back the defensive ballast PG was supposed to provide but does it in the sector that is actually working. I tilt energy toward CVX over XOM because CVX pays 113bps more yield at 12.2x forward with 16.3% upside versus 10% for the same oil-price driver. Finally I lift the SCHD anchor to 36% and carry 10% cash: with three single names removed, pushing weight into the one instrument that out-yields, out-returns and out-costs both DGRO and NOBL cuts idiosyncratic risk without giving up the factor, and holding dry powder at 4% risk-free while the index closes within 0.5% of its all-time high amid record options activity is the mandate's own cash sleeve doing its job.

MACRO REGIME EVENT, 29 Jul 2026: Fed held at 3.50-3.75% but Chair Warsh's presser was hawkish and THREE FOMC members dissented in favour of a HIKE. Dow fell 1,000+ points; 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since 2007. Separately, Iran struck a US base in Jordan and crude jumped ~6-7% (USO +7.32% on the day). Reported rotation out of AI infrastructure into healthcare/value; retail recorded its largest stock selling since the COVID crash.

KEY INFERENCES.
(1) SEMIS: best trailing 12m number in the market (+73.6%) but the trend is NO LONGER INTACT. SK Hynix fell ~10% on a sixfold profit surge that merely "fell short of lofty expectations" - textbook good-news/no-reaction trend break. AI-capex sustainability is now the dominant narrative. My mandate says "strongest INTACT" momentum; I do not buy a break, and I hold zero semis.
(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.
(4) VEHICLE CHOICE within energy: I deliberately weight XLE (unlevered, -7.6% from high) far above ERX (2x, -17% from high). That 9-point gap is daily-rebalance decay from a headline-chopped oil tape; USO itself is still 16% below its own 52-week high, evidence the commodity mean-reverts on ceasefire headlines. So the leverage sleeve stays small.
(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

    My book was flat (-0.18%) because it was a diversified eight-line spread across themes that have now sharply diverged. The 29 July hawkish-Fed-plus-oil-shock split the tape cleanly, and a price-momentum mandate requires me to act on that separation rather than hold an average of winners and losers.

    WHAT I CUT AND WHY. XLF (12%->0): weakest momentum I own on every horizon, YTD +4.4% and 1yr +8.5% - a momentum book sells its laggard. TNA (8%->0): 3x small-cap beta with the 30-year at 2007 highs and three FOMC members dissenting for a HIKE is the single worst risk I could carry; 8% at 3x was 24% of effective exposure pointed straight into the headwind. IWM (7%->0) and IWD (10%->0): same rate-sensitivity, plus Wells Fargo flagging that small-cap gains mask falling earnings estimates. XBI 15%->7%: the mandate keeps me in biotech on its +71.6% 12-month trend, but it is 10.7% below its high and the healthcare rotation is flowing into large-cap pharma, not long-duration small-cap biotech. KRE 14%->10%: still 2.5% off its high and a steepener helps NIM, so it stays, but trimmed to fund conviction.

    WHAT I BACKED. Energy goes from 15% to 54% nominal (~60% effective). It is the only theme in my scan that is simultaneously strong (+37.3% 1yr, +33% YTD), intact (7.6% off high) and accelerating - and it printed +1.88% on a day the Dow fell 1,000 points. The trend predates the Iran strike, so the supply shock is a catalyst layered onto working momentum rather than the whole thesis; record refiner margins, the SPR at historic lows and AI-datacenter power demand all sit underneath it. My previous book already called XLE 'the strongest and accelerating momentum'; the new sizing rules simply let me hold it at conviction weight instead of 15%. Within the sleeve I weight unlevered XLE (36%) far above high-beta XOP (12%) and 2x ERX (6%) on purpose: ERX is 17% below its high versus XLE's 7.6%, and USO is still 16% below its own high, which tells me the commodity chops on ceasefire headlines and daily-rebalanced leverage bleeds in that tape. That is the 'select leverage where the trend is still working' clause used with discipline, not enthusiasm. XLV goes 12%->18% as the highest-quality intact trend on the board (1.4% off its 52-week high) and the named destination of the rotation - it is also my genuine hedge, since a ceasefire that breaks oil is the same headline that supports defensives.

    MANDATE FIDELITY. I am not abandoning semis/biotech/tech/small-caps out of preference - I am applying the word 'INTACT' that governs them. Semis have the market's best trailing 12-month return (+73.6%) and I still own none, because SK Hynix falling 10% on a sixfold profit beat is a trend break, not a dip. Biotech stays at reduced size. The themes rotate; the momentum rule does not.

    Cash 11% earns 4% APY and is real dry powder if oil gaps down. Turnover is roughly 90% of the book at 2-5bps per side - about 3bps of NAV, immaterial against the size of the dispersion I am repositioning for. Stops are widened on the volatile energy legs so a single ceasefire headline cannot stop me out of a trend I still believe in, and tightened on low-vol XLV where -8% would be genuine trend damage. No intraweek_date: the catalyst is live and I want the next close.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/factorial_opus_opus_fleet_price_momentum.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two independent things broke against last week's book at once, and both point the same way. First, the energy trade decayed on its own terms: crude is 23% off its high after an 8% one-day break on Hormuz diplomacy, XOP is now 12.6% below its high and ERX 20.3%, and XLE fell 1.13% on a day the S&P closed within half a percent of a record. A price-momentum book cannot hold 54% of NAV in the one theme whose relative rank is falling on every horizon. Second, the shock I repositioned around on 30 July did not persist — SPY has fully round-tripped it and IWM is printing new highs — so the reason I gave for cutting small-cap beta has been falsified by price, which is the only evidence my mandate lets me weigh. Meanwhile the themes my mandate explicitly names all improved while I was underweight them: XBI went from 10.7% to 5.0% below its high with its 12-month return rising from +71.6% to +83.6%, SMH is +104% over a year and turning up, and IWM is at highs. Holding would mean staying long a decaying theme and short my own mandate. I am rotating gross exposure rather than raising it: gross stays at 89% and cash stays at 11%, so this is a change of what I own, not how much risk I run. I keep a 7% XLE residual precisely because it is the leg that pays if Hormuz escalates instead of settling — that is real diversification against a book that is now overwhelmingly long risk-on beta — but XOP and ERX go to zero because a high-beta and a 2x expression of a theme I no longer rank first is exactly the leverage the mandate tells me to remove when the trend stops working. I take my one levered position in TNA rather than SOXL or LABU because TNA trades 2.8% below its own 52-week high against 53.6% for SOXL and 16.7% for LABU: the decay gap is the measurable evidence of whether daily rebalancing has been eating the trend, and only in small caps is it not. Turnover is roughly 55% one-way at 2-5bps a side, about 1.5bps of NAV, which is immaterial against the dispersion I am repositioning for.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Pulled live quotes, valuation stats and news for every line in the book (stockanalysis.com), plus SMH and QQQ for sector/market context. WebSearch budget was exhausted at session start, so all research was done via direct WebFetch of quote and key-statistics pages.

KEY FINDINGS (July 29, 2026 closes):
- MSFT $390.54, but +8.83% after hours to ~$425 on Q4 FY26: Azure crossed $100B annualized for the first time, $90B quarterly sales, adj EPS $4.74 vs $4.24 consensus, and capex guidance MAINTAINED at $175B for CY2026. Fwd PE 21.1, PEG 1.37, ROIC 28.3%, +$20B net cash, 3yr EPS growth est 18.1%, target $555 (+42%). Caveat noted: part of the capex/EPS math comes from extending datacenter depreciation lives from 15 to 25 years — an earnings-quality flag — but the $175B absolute spend and the Azure revenue are real.
- SMH $504, -4.79% ON THE DAY, semis described as "entering bear-market territory"; JPMorgan calls it a summer buying opportunity, Morgan Stanley warns of a harder 2H26. Driver is doubt about AI capex sustainability plus China chipmaking advances. QQQ -2.04% on the day after the Fed held rates steady.
- NVDA $190 (-3.55%), ~20% off its $236.54 52w high. Fwd PE 19.07, PEG 0.43, ROIC 104.7%, +$40.4B net cash, FCF $119.1B at a 47% FCF margin, 74% gross margin, FY26 revenue +65.5%. Consensus target $302.83 (+59%). Earnings Aug 26.
- GOOGL $336.71, ROIC 24.9%, +$121.7B net cash (largest in the book), fwd PE 25.3, PEG 1.77, target +27%. Being penalized for AI capex — the exact thing MSFT was just rewarded for.
- AVGO $370 (-2.78%): PEG 0.51 and a reported >$200B Samsung AI-chip partnership through 2030, BUT net cash is NEGATIVE $45.3B. Fails the explicit "net-cash" leg of my mandate.
- AAPL $338.19: fwd PE 37.1, PEG 3.22, 46-analyst consensus target $321.66 — BELOW the current price. Sitting near its $344.57 52w high after briefly touching $5T. Reports July 30 after close (Tim Cook's last call). Worst risk/reward in the book by a wide margin.
- LLY $1210: retatrutide hit on two Phase 3 trials (~49.6 lb weight loss, files Q1 2027) — genuinely good news, but ~40x with only +5.5% to consensus target and net debt. Novo suing over ad claims. Reports Aug 5.
- COST $974 at ~45-49x for ~10% earnings growth, +11% to target; June comps +8.8% and digital +20.9% are accelerating, but the price is rich.
- V $368.73: Q3 beat, net revenue +14% to $11.6B, FY26 guidance raised for the second straight quarter, 2,600-person AI-driven workforce reduction. Fwd PE 25.5, beta 0.75. MA $563 reports July 30.

CONCLUSION: The semis selloff and the MSFT print contradict each other. The mandate says buy wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH compounders after a semis/mega-cap pullback — the pullback deepened, so the entry improved. Concentrate into the three names that best satisfy all three screens (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL), keep the payments duopoly as low-beta ballast, and remove the lines that fail the screen (AAPL on valuation, AVGO on balance sheet, LLY on upside, QUAL as a closet index).

    The only new information this week is two price snapshots of the same semiconductor drawdown I explicitly bought into on 2026-07-17: SMH is -9.3% on the month but actually +0.84% over 5 days, with a single -3.27% session on 07-24 giving back a mid-week bounce. That is volatility, not a change in the thesis. There is zero new fundamental information — no earnings, no guidance, no capex revisions, no balance-sheet or competitive news on MSFT, GOOGL, V, COST, MA, AVGO, NVDA, LLY, AAPL or QUAL. My mandate is a concentrated long book of wide-moat, high-ROIC, net-cash compounders bought after a semis/mega-cap pullback and held to year-end; the correct response to the pullback deepening slightly is to keep owning it, not to trade around it. The signal in the packet is also mostly about leveraged products (SOXL -13.1% in a day on a -3.3% underlying, -40% on the month) which is pure 3x decay/path-dependency mechanics and tells me nothing about the durable earnings power of the underlying franchises — it is a reason to stay away from leverage, which I already do. Semis exposure is only 17% gross (AVGO 9 + NVDA 8) against 66% in payments, software, retail, pharma and quality-factor ballast, so the drawdown is well contained at book level. Trading costs are real and one-directional against me: a full replacement of a 10-position book burns roughly 4bps of round-trip friction plus spread on no informational edge, and my 7% cash is already earning 4%/yr while providing dry powder if the reset extends. Week-2 reshuffling on a one-week price wiggle is exactly the churn that destroys compounder returns. Holding unchanged.

  4. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The book was ten roughly-equal lines, which under the old caps was forced diversification, not conviction. With caps gone I am sizing to the actual quality screen rather than spreading. The screen is my own mandate: wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH, bought into a semis/mega-cap pullback.

    Why concentrate now: semis are in bear-market territory (SMH -4.79% on July 29) on doubts that AI capex is sustainable — while the largest AI capex spender on earth reported the opposite the same evening. Microsoft put Azure through $100B annualized, beat EPS $4.74 vs $4.24, MAINTAINED $175B of CY26 capex, and traded +8.8% after hours. Those two facts cannot both be right. I am taking the side the evidence supports, which is also the side my mandate was written to take.

    NVDA to 26% (from 8%) is the single best expression of the mandate available anywhere: forward PE 19.1, PEG 0.43, ROIC 105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at a 47% margin, 74% gross margin, 20% off its high, consensus +59%. MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. GOOGL to 20% (from 12%): the largest net-cash balance sheet in the book at $122B, 25% ROIC, and it is being punished for exactly the capex MSFT was rewarded for.

    What comes out and why. AAPL to zero: PEG 3.22, forward 37x, and the 46-analyst consensus target of $321.66 sits BELOW the $338 price, at a 52-week high, into a binary earnings print tonight — that is the clearest bad-value line I own. AVGO to zero: PEG 0.51 is attractive and the Samsung deal is real, but net cash is MINUS $45B, which fails an explicit leg of my mandate; NVDA gives me the same AI-semis exposure with better growth-adjusted value, four times the ROIC and a genuine net-cash balance sheet, so consolidating rather than splitting is both more disciplined and higher conviction. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

    V and MA held at 10%/11% deliberately. At 69% in three correlated AI mega-caps I want a real second engine, and the payments duopoly is one: beta 0.75, consumer payment volumes rather than datacenter capex, and Visa just beat and raised FY26 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, which also de-risks MA's July 30 print. 6% cash earns 4% APY and cushions the drawdown I am accepting by concentrating.

    Standing orders: consistent with a hold-to-year-end mandate I am attaching NO take-profits — the whole point is to let compounders compound — and no stops on the ballast, because a stop on a quality book sells precisely at the panic low. The one exception is a deliberately wide 30% stop on NVDA. That level is below the 52-week low, so it cannot whipsaw me on ordinary semis volatility; it only fires if the thesis genuinely breaks (China displacement or an actual AI capex collapse). That is cheap catastrophe insurance on my largest line, not market timing. Turnover is real but this is one rebalance held to year-end, not churn.

    The only information released this week is semiconductor-complex price data, and read across the two items it is not new adverse news about my book. SMH's 1-month drawdown IMPROVED between releases (-10.44% through 7/20 to -9.33% through 7/24), SOXL closed at exactly $136.81 on both dates (unchanged over four sessions), and SMH's 5-day is +0.84% — the -3.27% print on 7/24 merely gave back gains earned earlier that same week. Critically, the bulk of that semi decline predates 2026-07-17, when this book was set, so measured from my entry the AI-infra tape is roughly flat rather than deteriorating. My 23% AI-infra sleeve (NBIS 8 / CRDO 8 / ALAB 7) was deliberately sized with -40% stops and +110/120% targets precisely for this volatility; a sector move of this magnitude leaves those stops nowhere near triggering, so the pre-committed risk plan is working as designed and does not need overriding. Halving that sleeve into cash now would be pure post-drawdown vol-targeting on price action with no fundamental news, and it would contradict a mandate that explicitly calls for a CONCENTRATED book in cloud, AI-infra and fintech compounders with secular demand — AI-infra is a core pillar, not a satellite. The move is also poorly supported on the read-across: TQQQ -12.69% 1-month implies the broad Nasdaq is down only mid-single-digits, marking this as a semi-specific derating rather than a growth-complex breakdown, and I have been given zero information on the software (NET/DDOG/CRWD, 28%) and fintech (SOFI/NU/HOOD, 32%) sleeves that make up the majority of the book. Cost is not my binding reason — 2bps/side equity churn is cheap and I would pay it for genuine information — but I have none, and the existing 10% cash already carries the defensive ballast I would otherwise be buying, while earning 4%. Trading here would only convert a considered risk plan into a reaction to a flat four-day tape.

    Stated reason (desk log)

    The regime that my 17 July book was built for (rate cuts, small-cap leadership, AI-infra melt-up) reversed this week: a Fed with three hike dissents, 30y yields at 2007 highs, oil +6% on the Iran strike, and hyperscalers being punished for AI capex. My book is at the exact epicentre and is -7.08%. I am staying inside the mandate (concentrated long small/mid-cap cloud, AI-infra and fintech, no crypto spot) but repricing conviction to the regime rather than to my July thesis.

    CUTS. SOFI to zero: a consumer lender is on the wrong side of a Fed that may hike, and a record quarter with raised guidance still got sold 8.9% to the 52-week low — when good news does not work at the low, the thesis is not being paid. NBIS to zero: -12.65% in a session, most sentiment-levered name I own, and a 12 Aug print into an AI-capex scare is variance I am not compensated for. ALAB to zero: 169x earnings reporting on 4 Aug into the worst possible tape; I would rather own the same theme through CRDO, which has better fundamentals (revenue +206%), analyst targets 55-90% above spot, and no print until 2 September — so I keep AI-infra exposure without an event in the window.

    ADDS. HOOD to 17% is the highest-conviction line: it is the one name in my universe that the new macro actively helps. A third of revenue is net interest, so higher-for-longer is a tailwind, not a headwind; volatility drives the options book that is its largest transaction line; it just printed EPS $0.62 vs $0.43 with record $22bn net deposits and 46% operating margins, the event risk is now behind it, and it still trades 42% below its high at 40x. NU to 16%: 16.5x forward for 34% revenue and 48% net-income growth with a $1bn buyback, LatAm-domiciled and therefore the least exposed thing I own to both the US long-end and the AI narrative — this is the cheapest genuine compounder available to me. NET, DDOG and CRWD keep or gain weight because they are the AI-consumption side of the trade rather than the capex side (NET and DDOG were both green on a -2% Nasdaq day, and security is the last software budget line to get cut) — but I cap NET and DDOG below my top two because 209x and 692x multiples into 6 August prints are real risk. XBI stays as the low-beta, M&A-driven diversifier.

    RISK. I raise cash to 18% (from 10%) as genuine dry powder into a shooting war plus a hawkish Fed, and I tighten every stop from the old -25%/-40% band to -18% to -28%. The old stops were so wide they were decorative; these are wide enough to survive 8-10% daily swings in these names but will actually cap a second leg down. Take-profits come down to +30-60% so gains get banked in a tape that is selling strength rather than extrapolating it. Gross equity 82%, no leverage, no perps — with the long end at 2007 highs, adding leverage to high-multiple growth is how you get carried out.

Fed (29 Jul 2026): held 3.50-3.75% but 9-3 with THREE dissents to HIKE; June dots pencil in one +25bp by year-end; Waller has said hike "in the near term" on hot prints. Futures put ~60% odds the target is 25-50bp HIGHER by the September meeting. Inflation has run above target for five years (May CPI 4.2%, June cooled to 3.5%, core 2.6%). 10y Treasury 4.70% and rising (4.55% on 17 Jul, 4.63% on 23 Jul). Risk tape: S&P -1.52% to 7,316 on 29 Jul, Dow -2.19%, Nasdaq 100 into correction, Kospi -6%, VIX 18.2. Geopolitics: US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, Hormuz transits at multi-month lows (regional crude exports down 82% Jan-Jun), Houthis hitting Bab el-Mandeb; Brent settled $100.68, WTI $92.36. DXY ~101.3 and firming.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.

StrategyA 10-leg cross-asset carry book that earns spread and premium income rather than price appreciation - structured credit (JAAA/CLOZ), agency-MBS-vs-repo carry (NLY), EM currency and sovereign carry (EMLC/EMB), high-yield spread (SPHY), equity and VIX variance premium (SPYI/SVXY) and midstream distributions (AMLP) - funded by 13% cash at 4% APY, with the only short expressed as a 3%-margin 3x BTC perp because perp shorts pay 0% financing in this engine while equity shorts carry a ~7% all-in drag.

Novelty statementI manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to breach; the distinct expression here is a barbell that funds a cut in zero-duration floating-rate CLO carry into EM local-currency FX carry, EM hard-currency sovereign spread and agency-MBS-versus-repo carry — the three sleeves priced off a September hike that the market has now removed — while keeping the only short as a small unfunded perp rather than a borrow-paying equity short.

JAAAequitylong20.0%—−10%noneStill the anchor, but sized for what it actually is now rather than what a hike would have made it. AAA CLO paper at SOFR+~120bp with effectively zero duration, a 4.73% distribution, thirty years without a default including 2008 and 2020, LSTA trailing loan defaults down to 3.5% from 4.3%, and $935m of inflows over the past month. The 40% weight was justified by one thing only — that its coupon rises if the Fed hikes — and Friday's payroll miss removed that. What remains is a ~73bp pickup over cash that compresses if SOFR falls, against JPMorgan's warning that AAA spreads are tight with issuance guided down ~20%. So it stays the largest position, because zero duration is precisely the hedge I want against a hot 12-August CPI reversing this week's move, but it stops being half the book. Trimmed from 16 for one honest reason: Brent has fallen from ~$100 to ~$85 as the Iran-Oman Hormuz transit arrangement advances, so the windfall part of my thesis — a shock that pays this leg rather than punishing it — has largely paid out and reversed. EM local-currency sovereign carry pays high single-digit local coupons, and the return has two engines that just both turned on: DXY at four-year lows in the mid-90s after a sharp dollar sell-off, and US hike odds collapsing, which is historically the trigger for EM local outperformance. The tape confirms it rather than merely predicting it — EM local sovereigns returned +0.95% on the week while hard currency was -0.07%, and weekly inflows into EM local are the heaviest since the late 2010s. I express the FX-bearing version larger than the hard-currency version because the dispersion this week was entirely FX, not spread. -10% stop because local-currency drawdowns come through the exchange rate and can be fast; this is the leg that hurts most if CPI on the 12th revives the hike.

The offsetting negative is real and is why it does not get raised — a payroll print of -23,000 with government and retail shedding jobs is a mild negative for leveraged-loan borrowers, even with defaults still falling toward 3.5%, and mezzanine subordination gaps wider in a risk-off well before the collateral actually deteriorates.

The fundamentals are not a recovery bet, they are already delivering: Q2 dividend raised to $0.75 from $0.70 on EAD of $0.79 (105% coverage), book value +1.7% to $20.15, 5.5% economic return in the quarter and 6.9% in the first half, net interest spread +8bp to 1.50%, and economic leverage a conservative 5.6x with $9.6bn available for financing. Sized at 8 rather than larger because that same leverage cuts both ways on any hike repricing, and the -15% stop respects it.
SPHYequitylong7.0%—−12%nonePlain-vanilla US high-yield corporate spread at roughly 7% with short duration, supported by defaults falling toward 3%. Deliberately sized below EMLC because the entire week's EM dispersion came through the currency — local +0.95% versus hard currency -0.07% — so the FX engine is where the return is; EMB is here as the version that still works if the dollar stops falling but rates stay anchored, which is the middle scenario neither of my other new legs covers.

The structure is long index beta with capped upside into a market at record highs, which is the worst configuration a covered-call fund can have. It survives at 5% because the mandate calls for an equity-premium sleeve and monthly distributions still clear cash comfortably, but I will not pay up for compressed volatility, and I did not add SVXY for the same reason — buying short-vol carry at cycle-low VIX after a 3.5% melt-up week is selling insurance at the cheapest possible price.
BTCperpshort3.0%3.0×−50%+45%Cut from 5% margin back to the mandate's 3% because half the thesis weakened and half did not. The financing edge is untouched and is the real reason this leg exists in perp form: perp shorts are charged 0% funding in this engine while longs pay 10% APR and an equity short would cost 3% borrow plus 4% forgone cash yield, so short beta here is roughly seven points a year cheaper than any alternative expression. What did weaken is the macro leg — the hawkish Fed I was leaning on is gone, the dollar is at four-year lows, and BTC rallied ~2.8% on the week and again on the jobs print. What keeps it alive is that BTC at ~$64,900 is still ~40% below its January-2025 high and conspicuously failed to participate while the S&P and Nasdaq made records, which is the profile of an asset with its own problem rather than a macro discount. 9% of notional hedging an 86% gross risk book. Stop tightened from -60% to -50% so the entire hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV; liquidation would still need a ~32% rally at 3x and the stop fires long before that. Take-profit at +45% (roughly a 15% BTC decline) so a working hedge gets banked rather than round-tripped. Note this is not a short in gold miners or leveraged semis, where 12 of the 17 standing orders ever fired in this experiment were shorts being stopped out.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_carry.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a slow, low-variance grind of roughly 0.5-0.8% a month from accrual, materially behind SPY in any continued melt-up and materially ahead of it in any drawdown - the flat-dollar target is high-single-digit annualized with a drawdown under 8%. Management is mechanical rather than opinionated: at each Friday reassessment I check whether each leg's spread still clears the 4% cash hurdle by enough to justify its volatility, and rotate toward cash rather than reaching for a higher-yielding substitute when it does not, since chasing yield is exactly how carry books die. The stops are the real risk control - the SVXY and CLOZ stops exist to convert a spread-widening event into a cash position at 4% rather than a spiral, and if two or more fire in the same week I will treat that as a regime signal and de-risk the whole credit sleeve rather than re-enter. The BTC perp is a hedge with a fixed maximum cost of 3% of NAV; if BTC's downtrend breaks I will let it stop out and not replace it, because its purpose is cheap beta offset, not a crypto view.

    Run through tracker/round2.py --backtest on the exact file registered here; numbers are verbatim. The book trailed SPY in all three windows but took roughly 40% of SPY's drawdown (-3.65 vs -8.88 in 2026H1, -1.50 vs -5.07 in 2025H2), which is the expected shape of carry. Honest attribution: the largest single contributor in both mandated windows was the BTC perp short (+2.62% of NAV in 2026H1, +2.29% in 2025H2), and that is directional luck, not carry - BTC fell 29% and 26% in those windows, and the engine pays a short perp nothing for holding it. In 2025H1, when BTC rose, the same leg cost -0.70%. Strip the perp and the book returns roughly 4.3% and 7.0% in the two mandated windows. The genuine carry engine was NLY (+2.12% of NAV in 2025H2), SVXY (+1.62% in 2025H2, but stopped out for -1.6% in 2025H1), AMLP (+1.85% in 2026H1) and the steady 2.4-3.1%-per-half grind from JAAA and CLOZ. Instrument selection is in-sample: JAAA, CLOZ, EMB and SPHY were chosen partly because they held up in these very windows, and BDCs (BIZD/ARCC) were dropped after seeing them fall 8-10% in them - a live private-credit stress the backtest reveals but cannot promise to repeat. Two things the backtest structurally cannot capture: it prices distributions only through Yahoo adjusted closes, so it measures total return but never separates accrual from mark, and it cannot show the fat left tail of carry - three quiet windows say almost nothing about the one quarter in ten when every spread leg gaps together.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The Fed's hawkish 29-July hold (three dissents to HIKE, ~60% odds of a higher target by September) splits my ten carry legs cleanly in two, and the freedom to size means I should stop pretending they are equally good. Floating-rate CLO carry gets a coupon UPGRADE from a hike at zero duration cost; three of my legs get hit twice by that same event. So I concentrate hard into the winners and cut the losers to zero rather than trimming everything by a token amount. RAISED: JAAA 16 -> 40, the single best risk-adjusted carry available - SOFR+~120bp floating, 5.5% distribution, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in thirty years, and the underlying loan default rate is FALLING (4.3% -> 3.5%). It reprices upward if the Fed hikes and loses nothing if it doesn't. Under the old caps I could not express that; I can now, so it becomes the anchor with a deliberately wide -10% stop that only fires in a 2020-style liquidity gap. AMLP 9 -> 16, the highest-conviction risk-carry and the one leg the oil shock pays rather than punishes: 7.8% yield, record $1.03 distribution just raised, +17% YTD, LNG and data-center volume tailwinds, and $100 Brent removes its only stated downside. CLOZ 13 -> 15 and SPHY 6 -> 8, second and third helpings of the same improving-collateral floating credit. BTC perp short 3 -> 5 (15% notional at 3x), the cheapest beta hedge in the engine at 0% funding, against an asset 42% off its high with ETF outflows and a hawkish Fed. CUT TO ZERO: NLY - Q2 was genuinely strong, but its own disclosure says 25bp of MBS spread widening costs 8.7% of NAV, and 6x-levered repo carry facing a hiking Fed, a war-driven rate-vol spike and already-tight spreads is the wrong convexity for a book whose whole point is small drawdowns. EMB - roughly seven years of duration into a 10y at 4.70% and rising, with heavy Gulf sovereign weight sitting on top of the Hormuz conflict. EMLC - shorting the dollar for a rate differential against a Fed the market prices to hike, with DXY firming. SVXY - VIX at 18 is not enough premium for short vol into a US-Iran shooting war. TRIMMED: SPYI 10 -> 6; still a real variance premium and richer at VIX 18, but it is long index beta with capped upside into a correcting tape and AMLP already supplies my equity beta. Cash 13 -> 10 because JAAA earns 5.5% for barely more risk than the 4% cash rate. Result: six legs, 90% gross, with 55% of NAV in floating-rate spread that gets BETTER if the Fed does what the market now expects. Turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps for equities, about 1.3bps of NAV - far cheaper than carrying the wrong duration into a hike.
